diagnostics.title: Buffer pool: full or warming
diagnostics.headline: Warming: 31% full
diagnostics.verdict: The buffer pool is still filling: 30.9% of it is in use (5,661 of 8,192 pages are free). It did not grow in this window. Reads from disk are expected while it warms.
diagnostics.why: InnoDB keeps a small free list: while the server is busy, its page cleaner evicts the least recently used pages until each buffer pool instance has innodb_lru_scan_depth free pages, and an idle full pool can show 0 free pages (1,024 x 1 = 1,024 pages here). So "full" means free pages at or below that target, not zero. Once it is full, every page read from disk evicts another one. Bytes read from disk are the pages read from disk times innodb_page_size (16.0 KiB); MySQL adds Innodb_buffer_pool_read_ahead, because Innodb_buffer_pool_reads leaves out linear read-ahead. Innodb_data_read counts the bytes InnoDB read from its data files: it is lower for ROW_FORMAT=COMPRESSED tables, which read the smaller compressed page, and on MySQL it also counts redo log reads, but only during startup.
diagnostics.rule: full when free pages are at or below innodb_lru_scan_depth x buffer pool instances (the free list InnoDB's page cleaner keeps). Full: ok below 10 pages read from disk per second, watch at 10 or more, problem when the hit ratio is also below 95%. Not full: no threshold

diagnostics.title: Redo log size for the write rate
diagnostics.headline: No redo in this window
diagnostics.verdict: InnoDB wrote no redo in the window. The checkpoint age is 0 B (0% of the capacity).
diagnostics.why: InnoDB writes every change to the redo log first. A checkpoint frees redo space once the matching dirty pages are flushed, so the capacity limits how far flushing can fall behind. The checkpoint age (Innodb_redo_log_current_lsn minus Innodb_redo_log_checkpoint_lsn) is how much of the capacity is in use. MySQL's redo-driven adaptive flushing starts early (about 8% of the capacity, innodb_adaptive_flushing_lwm) and grows with the age, reaches its age limit at about 73%, forces flushing from about 79% (innodb_flush_sync, on by default), and makes user writes wait from about 84%. These points compare the age of the oldest dirty page, which is at most the checkpoint age. A larger redo log smooths that out but makes crash recovery longer. Two counters measure redo. The log sequence number (Innodb_redo_log_current_lsn) grows by the redo generated, counted in 512-byte log blocks including their headers and trailers; it is what fills the capacity, so the times are computed from it. Innodb_os_log_written counts the bytes written to the redo files: the log writer rewrites the last, partly filled block on each write, so with many small commits it runs well above the redo generated. Innodb_log_waits counts waits for space in the in-memory log buffer (innodb_log_buffer_size), a different limit.
diagnostics.rule: watch when the checkpoint age reaches about 73% of the capacity (where adaptive flushing reaches its age limit) in either sample, problem at about 79% (forced flushing); also watch when the capacity holds less than about 1 hour of redo at this window's rate (a common rule of thumb; this window may not be the peak) or when Innodb_log_waits grew

diagnostics.title: Table open cache
diagnostics.headline: No misses
diagnostics.verdict: No overflows in the window: the tables in use fit in the cache. 0.0% of 1 lookups missed. 537 of 4,000 cached instances are open.
diagnostics.why: Each statement needs an open instance of every table it uses. A hit reuses a free instance from the cache. A miss opens a new one (Opened_tables): the first use of a table, or another session needing its own instance of a busy table, so misses alone are normal. An overflow means the cache was full and an unused instance was closed to make room: tables are being opened and closed over and over. MySQL divides table_open_cache across table_open_cache_instances.
diagnostics.rule: watch at 1 overflow per second, problem at 10, with at least 5 in the window. Misses without overflows are not judged

diagnostics.title: Table definition cache
diagnostics.headline: 0 opened per second
diagnostics.verdict: 0 table definitions were opened in the window (0 per second); 94 of 2,000 are cached.
diagnostics.why: The definition cache keeps parsed table definitions (shares), separate from the open table instances. A definition is opened the first time a table is used, or again after it was evicted because the cache was full. Steady openings while the cache is full mean table_definition_cache is smaller than the number of tables in use.
diagnostics.rule: watch when table definitions are opened at 1 per second or more (at least 5 in the window) while the definition cache is at least 95% full

diagnostics.title: Thread pool
diagnostics.headline: 20 threads, 19 idle
diagnostics.verdict: thread_handling is pool-of-threads, so Percona Server's thread pool runs statements on worker threads in thread_pool_size 16 thread groups (about that many statements execute at once) instead of one thread per connection, and the thread cache does not apply. It has 20 worker threads now, 19 of them idle, at most 100,000.
diagnostics.why: With one thread per connection, the server keeps up to thread_cache_size idle threads to reuse for new connections; Threads_created counts the threads it had to create instead. Connections is the next thread id: every connection that got past the max_connections check (failed logins included), plus a few internal threads. Each window includes this tool's own connection.
diagnostics.rule: No threshold: compare with this server's usual values

diagnostics.title: Binary log cache
diagnostics.headline: No binary log writes
diagnostics.verdict: No transaction wrote to the binary log in the window.
diagnostics.why: With the binary log on, each session collects a transaction's events in memory (binlog_cache_size; binlog_stmt_cache_size for changes to non-transactional tables) and writes them to the binary log at commit. Events that do not fit spill to a temporary file on disk (Binlog_cache_disk_use, Binlog_stmt_cache_disk_use). The cache is per session, so a larger size is multiplied by the sessions that write.
diagnostics.rule: watch when 10% or more of the transactions or statements that used a binary log cache spilled to a temporary file, with at least 5 spills in the window; never a problem

numbers.label: Non-transactional statements that spilled to disk

diagnostics.title: Open files
diagnostics.headline: 0.0% of open_files_limit
diagnostics.verdict: At least 34 file descriptors are in use: 3 through the server's file layer, 30 InnoDB files and 1 connection, 0.0% of open_files_limit 1,048,576.
diagnostics.why: open_files_limit is the most file descriptors the server process can hold. Open_files counts files the server opened through its own file layer (MyISAM and Aria tables, binary and relay logs, some temporary files), not InnoDB's, which Innodb_num_open_files counts; each client connection also uses a socket. myflames adds the three, a lower bound: other descriptors are not visible through SQL.
diagnostics.rule: watch when the file descriptors myflames can account for reach 75% of open_files_limit, problem at 90%

diagnostics.title: Rows read by full scans
diagnostics.headline: 531 rows/s by sequential scans
diagnostics.verdict: Storage engines returned 531 rows per second to sequential scans, 100.0% of all rows read through handlers.
diagnostics.why: Handler_read_rnd_next counts requests for the next row of a sequential table scan, so a high rate points at full table scans. It also counts scans of internal temporary tables (GROUP BY, DISTINCT, derived tables, UNION), and this tool's own SHOW GLOBAL STATUS reads about 1,000 rows that way per window (measured), so it is an upper bound on rows from full scans of user tables. Full index scans count in Handler_read_first and Handler_read_next instead. Top statements shows which statements scan.
diagnostics.rule: No threshold: compare with this server's usual values

numbers.label: Share of all rows read through handlers

diagnostics.title: Temporary tables on disk
diagnostics.headline: 0.0% of 1 on disk
diagnostics.verdict: 0 of 1 internal temporary tables in the window were on disk (0.0%).
diagnostics.why: Internal temporary tables (GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION, derived tables) start in memory and move to disk when they outgrow the limit. TempTable keeps each internal temporary table in memory up to tmp_table_size (16.0 MiB), and all of them up to temptable_max_ram (1.0 GiB) together; on disk they are InnoDB tables. TempTable overflow into memory-mapped files (temptable_max_mmap) is not counted as disk.
diagnostics.rule: watch at 10% on disk, problem at 25%; with fewer than 20 temporary tables in the window, watch at most

numbers.label: Created on disk or moved there

settings.name: temptable_max_ram
settings.default: 3% of memory, 1 to 4 GiB (8.4 to 9.5); 1 GiB from 9.6 unless server_memory is set

diagnostics.title: Sorts that spill to disk
diagnostics.headline: 0 merge passes for 0 sorts
diagnostics.verdict: 0 merge passes in the window for 0 sorts. Sorts fit in sort_buffer_size.
diagnostics.why: A sort that cannot use an index (filesort) collects rows in sort_buffer_size. When they do not fit, it writes sorted runs to a temporary file and merges them, and each merge pass is counted in Sort_merge_passes. Sort_range and Sort_scan count the sorts themselves. sort_buffer_size is a limit for each sort in every session, so raise it for the sessions that need it rather than globally.
diagnostics.rule: watch at 1 per second, problem at 10 per second, with at least 5 in the window

metrics.label: Buffer pool hit ratio
metrics.explain: Share of page requests InnoDB served from memory over the window, without reading the page from disk. MySQL counts linear read-ahead only in Innodb_buffer_pool_read_ahead, so it is added; disk reads are the sum.
metrics.why: Only 0 page requests in the window, too few to judge. No threshold: compare with this server's usual values.

metrics.label: Dirty pages
metrics.explain: Pages changed in memory and not yet flushed to disk, as a share of the buffer pool. Near innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct (90%) InnoDB flushes harder. A high share alone is not a stall; waits for a free page and a nearly full redo log are. MySQL starts flushing gradually at innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct_lwm (10 by default).
metrics.why: 0 of 8,192 pages are dirty. Rule of thumb: watch at innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct; a high share alone is not a stall, waits for a free page and a nearly full redo log are.
metrics.rule: watch at innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct; a high share alone is not a stall, waits for a free page and a nearly full redo log are

metrics.label: Free pages
metrics.explain: Empty pages ready for new reads. A busy server's buffer pool is usually full, which is normal: InnoDB evicts the least recently used pages. Waits for a free page are the signal.
metrics.why: 5,661 of 8,192 pages are free. No threshold: compare with this server's usual values.

metrics.label: Waits for a free page
metrics.explain: Times a session found no free page, even after scanning the LRU list, so it had to flush a page or wait (Innodb_buffer_pool_wait_free; MySQL counts each retry). The page cleaner is not keeping up, or the buffer pool is small for the workload.
metrics.why: 0 waits in 2 s (0 per second). Rule of thumb: watch when any occur in the window, problem at 1 per second or more.
metrics.rule: watch when any occur in the window, problem at 1 per second or more

metrics.label: Redo generated
metrics.explain: Redo log generated per second (Innodb_redo_log_current_lsn, the log sequence number's growth). MySQL's adaptive flushing reaches its age limit when the checkpoint age is about 73% of the redo capacity, and MariaDB flushes ahead from 7/8 of Innodb_checkpoint_max_age (about 71% of innodb_log_file_size), so the time shown runs from the current checkpoint age to that point. Writes stall if the log fills before a checkpoint frees it.
